newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil FDI to rise in '97, but c/a gap to widen too.
newsitem.headline: Brazil FDI to rise in '97, but c/a gap to widen too.

text.p: Foreign direct investment in Brazil is expected to soar to new record levels in 1997, but the country's current account gap is also likely to widen, pressured by trade and services, a Central Bank official said.
Altamir Lopes, head of the bank's economics department, declined in a news conference to put firm numbers on either foreign investment (FDI) or the current account this year.

But he said, "investment will be higher than in 1996" and acknowledged that "it seems" 1997's trade gap and interest payments on overseas debt would also be up, putting pressure on the current account.
Brazil posted a current account deficit of 3.27 percent of gross domestic product last year, the widest gap since 1983 and above government estimates of a 3.0 percent of GDP deficit.
In 1995, the gap was a much lower 2.47 percent of GDP.
Economic analysts said that though slightly on the high side, the 1996 current account result was within expectations.
Lopes said the numbers were "nothing special" when record FDI of $9.442 billion in 1996 was taken into account.
"What is important is that this investment is financing 38.8 percent of the deficit when in 1995 foreign investment only financed about 22 percent," he said.
Industry and Commerce Minister Francisco Dornelles said in a newspaper interview published Friday that he expected $16 billion in foreign direct investment this year, nearly twice as much as in 1996.

Much of the new foreign funding will be drawn by Brazil's privatization programme, expected to peak this year with the sale of the jewel in Brasilia's crown, mining colossus Companhia Vale do Rio Doce. That auction alone should raise some $6.0 billion, Planning Minister Antonio Kandir said late last year.

The balance of Brazil's current account gap not covered by foreign investment amounted to about $14.91 billion in 1996, which Lopes said was easily financed by short-term capital and overseas borrowings.

Net inflows from short-term portfolio investment amounted to $6.12 billion while overseas borrowing through debt issues was $21.6 billion, allowing the Central Bank to predict a comfortable balance of payments surplus.
Lopes said the balance of payments result for 1996 would be made available next month and should show a surplus of about $8.0 billion.
The Brazilian Central Bank's Internet page, which should carry the 1996 balance of payments results within a few days, is available at http://www.bcb.gov.br
